newsitem.title: ITALY: Albania force may have to stay past elections - Italy. [corrected 12:00 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Albania force may have to stay past elections - Italy. [corrected 12:00 gmt]

text.p: (Corrects headline and first paragraph to make clear possible time frame.)

A multinational security force being assembled for Albania may have to stay in the Balkan country beyond elections planned for June, Italy's Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta was quoted as saying on Friday.

The Italian-led force of up to 6,000 men, which could start to deploy late next week, received United Nations authorisation on March 28 under a Security Council mandate that runs for an initial three months.

"The U.N. has set this time scale but it is clear that if this military and electoral cycle requires four or five months, it is probable that the U.N. will extend the mandate," Andreatta told La Stampa newspaper.
The force, from at least eight nations, is meant to protect relief deliveries to impoverished Albania after order broke down in much of the south following an armed uprising last month.
Early elections are planned by the end of June under a deal reached by Albanian political parties that set up a national unity government led by opposition Socialist Bashkim Fino.

Much of the south is in the hands of rebel committees calling for the resignation of rightist President Sali Berisha, whom insurgents blame for the loss of tens of thousands of people's savings in shady pyramid investment schemes.

Berisha told Corriere della Sera newspaper in an interview in Tirana that he regarded the rebel committees as "a mixture of traffickers and mafiosi" backed by supporters of the Stalinist regime that collapsed in Albania in 1990.

"I cannot exclude a risk (to the force). There are a lot of armed criminals around who are capable of causing harm. However, the risk is not very high and the mission concerns all of Albania," he was quoted as saying.

The force is seen as crucial to stabilising the country and ensuring that the June election takes place. It is also aimed at heading off any further mass movement of illegal immigrants to Italy and Greece.

So far, Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400. Austria and Bulgaria have also said they are prepared to contribute troops.

Senior diplomats from contributor countries were meeting in Rome on Friday to establish a political framework for the force, whose deployment is being planned by military experts meeting separately in the Italian capital.
The force is expected to secure the ports of Durres and Vlore, the latter in rebel hands, as well as Tirana airport and key transport routes.
Italy's chief of defence staff, Admiral Guido Venturoni, said the operation would require 5,000 to 6,000 men on the ground "to restore a minimum of order in a reasonable time".
The biggest risk to the force came from lawless gangs, he told Corriere della Sera newspaper.

"Let's be clear about this. The situation there is already improving a great deal. But if there weren't risks there would be no reason to go there," Venturoni said. "If anyone attacks us it is clear that we will respond," he added.

Venturoni said it would be up to Albanian police and not the security force to disarm Albanians who have seized huge quantities of small arms after protesters stormed weapons depots last month and put police and soldiers to flight.
